one_liner: Asana is buildable now as an agent toolkit using a free account and its documented REST API.

auth.notes: OAuth is recommended for apps supporting multiple users. Personal access tokens are also documented; Enterprise service-account tokens require a super admin.

access.notes: A free Asana account can be used to test the API. The optional developer sandbox requires a request, and App Directory publication has a separate review process.

api.notes: The public reference documents operations across core work-management objects.

mcp.notes: Asana documents an available hosted V2 server. The separate V1 server is deprecated.

verdict.rationale: Asana documents free-account API testing and token-based authentication, with a public REST reference covering work-management objects. The requested sandbox and App Directory review are not prerequisites to testing the API.

evidence.quote: You will likely want to use OAuth if your app needs to support multiple users signing in to use the app.
A personal access token (PAT) is the quickest and simplest way to authenticate in the API.
Service Accounts are an Enterprise tier feature and can only be created by Asana super admins (see more about admin roles at Asana ).
You can test in any of your existing workspaces, create a free account, or request a developer sandbox .
The quickest method to do so is by using a personal access token (PAT), which you can think of as your unique password for accessing the API.
To see the feature differences between the Asana plans, please visit our pricing page . ➡ To request a developer sandbox, please complete and submit this form .
Set your distribution to “any workspace”, then follow the instructions on the Developer Console > Submit for Review page.
This reference is generated from our OpenAPI Specification , and contains a comprehensive reference for objects, schemas, and endpoints available in the API.
The Asana API is a RESTful interface with predictable resource-oriented URLs, accepts JSON or form-encoded requests, returns JSON, and uses standard HTTP features (verbs, response codes, etc.)
These same operations that you performed on a task through the API can be applied to many other objects in your Asana instance as well (e.g., projects , portfolios , etc.).
Asana offers a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants and other applications to access the Asana Work Graph.
The Asana MCP V2 server is available at: https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp . This server requires authentication with your Asana account.
Use your own Asana app when you want users to see your app's name on the consent screen and control the credentials yourself.

problems: No material documentation wall encountered. The optional sandbox’s approval and provisioning should not be confused with the free-account route to API credentials.
name: Asana

verification.note: OAuth is documented for apps with multiple users, and a personal access token is documented as the simplest API credential, which fairly counts as bearer_token. Primary oauth2 matches the multi-user recommendation; the enterprise service-account restriction is also quoted.

A free account is an explicit way to test the API, with a PAT as the quickest credential, so self_serve_free is proven. The sandbox form and App Directory review are quoted as separate, optional steps.

The API is explicitly RESTful, JSON-based, and publicly documented at the cited reference. A comprehensive endpoint reference plus operations on tasks, projects, and portfolios supports broad breadth and does not contradict it.
Asana itself offers a hosted MCP server and states the V2 URL is available, supporting official and generally_available. No quote shows that a separate V1 server is deprecated.
The quote is on a Composio toolkit page for Asana and discusses using an Asana app, so catalog listing is shown.
Self-serve free credentials plus a documented, broad public REST API meet buildable_now with main_blocker none. Sandbox requests and App Directory review are not required to test the API.
